to reform something is to alter it

explanation.definitionFit: A psalter is the book of Psalms used in worship, a standard church text.

clue.text: Pores over a child's first bits of artwork, messily clutched

the opening letter of each word

explanation.definitionFit: Stomata are the tiny openings in the surface of leaves through which plants exchange gases.

clue.text: Final one to finish admitted not being this, as the saying goes?

the closing letter of the word

explanation.definitionFit: The proverb 'last but not least' says the final item is not the smallest, so the answer is the word the last one is not.

clue.text: Formerly healthy, daughter had a blow-out?

blocks.note: ex- means former
hale means robustly healthy
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A once-healthy daughter went on a binge or had a tyre burst.
explanation.walkthrough: A blow-out usually means a big feast or a burst tyre; here it is just breathing out.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhale is to breathe out, a literal blowing out of air, so the past tense fits.

clue.text: It's all eyes on this popinjay!

definitions.text: It's all eyes on this popinjay!

blocks.clueFragment: It's all eyes on this popinjay!
blocks.note: surface reading: everyone is staring at this show-off
setter's reading: the bird's tail feathers are covered in eye-like markings

explanation.surface: A vain dandy who loves being the centre of attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All eyes on' sounds like an audience watching, but it is literal: the bird's fanned tail is patterned with eyespots.
explanation.definitionFit: A popinjay is a vain, strutting person, and the showy bird with an eyespotted tail is the classic emblem of vanity.

clue.text: Catch lover, bound up, getting his end away

explanation.surface: A saucy tale of a lover tied up and having his way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting his end away' is British slang for having sex; here it means dropping the last letter of the lover.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrap is to catch someone by trickery or in a trap.

clue.text: Very happy to stake a birdhouse for the Reverend

taken as written
a coop houses hens; it takes its opening sound from the pawning word

explanation.surface: A vicar delighted to bet on a henhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of HOCK and COOP to get the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Cock-a-hoop is an idiom for exultant, crowing with delight.

clue.text: Take part not all of whole (missing fifth)

blocks.note: something whole is complete

explanation.surface: A puzzled note about joining in with only part of something.
explanation.definitionFit: To compete is to take part in a contest, such as a race or match.

clue.text: Be free to be a nudist

blocks.note: first meaning: to have no engagements in one's diary
second meaning: to wear no clothes at all

explanation.surface: Freedom defined as going without clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase means both 'no plans' and 'no clothes'.
explanation.definitionFit: Having no appointments leaves one free, and wearing no garments is what a naturist does.

clue.text: Free-for-all in these meetings? Quite the reverse!

indicators.note: the clue says these meetings contain the phrase; flipping that claim means the meetings sit inside the phrase instead

blocks.note: the letters run across the middle of the hyphenated phrase

explanation.surface: A joke that these gatherings are anything goes, then a sly retraction.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the first half backwards in sense: not 'free-for-all in meetings' but 'meetings in free-for-all'. FORA is the Latin plural of forum.
explanation.definitionFit: Fora are forums, gatherings held for open public discussion, so the plural fits 'meetings'.

clue.text: That chap touring calm path in fitness retreat

the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A man on a walking holiday at a wellness resort.

clue.text: Might her novels go here?

blocks.note: surface reading: the books of some woman novelist, and where they should be shelved
setter's reading: the shelf above a fireplace shares its name with the author of Wolf Hall

explanation.surface: Wondering where a particular woman's books should be kept.
explanation.walkthrough: Hilary Mantel wrote the Wolf Hall novels; 'her' refers to her, and the answer is the shelf over the fireplace where books might stand.
explanation.definitionFit: A mantel is the shelf above a fireplace, a spot for ornaments and books, and it is also the surname of the novelist.

clue.text: Discharges drunk men at sea

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

clue.text: In Cornwall, Catholic assumes a belief that can't be questioned

indicators.note: in with a place means everything else is placed inside that place's abbreviation

blocks.note: Cornwall lies in the South West of England

C is a standard abbreviation for Catholic

explanation.surface: A Cornish Catholic taking on an unquestionable article of faith.
explanation.walkthrough: C goes inside A CREDO, and that whole lot goes inside SW, the region containing Cornwall, England's south-western tip.
explanation.definitionFit: A sacred cow is an idea or institution treated as beyond criticism, like the animal revered in Hinduism.

clue.text: Thinking back to being exhausted after record breaking finisher

indicators.note: the finisher of a word is its closing letter

blocks.note: REC is a common abbreviation for record
all in means tired out
the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: An athlete remembering how drained they felt after a record-breaking finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts ALL IN behind REC. 'Record breaking finisher' looks like one phrase about a winning athlete.
explanation.definitionFit: Recalling something means calling it back to mind, which is thinking back.

clue.text: In film, sounds like a little horse? Sounds like it!

blocks.note: like a foal, a little horse

explanation.surface: A film question about horse noises, answered with a wink.
explanation.walkthrough: The closing exclamation also hints at what Foley artists do: create sounds, such as coconut-shell hoofbeats, that mimic the real thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Foley is the craft of adding everyday sound effects to a film after shooting, named after Jack Foley.

clue.text: Might one feature dapper hat and cane-twirling?

definitions.text: Might one feature dapper hat and cane-twirling?

twirling spins things round, so the letters are turned into a new order

the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Picturing a top-hat-and-cane routine on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: a song-and-dance number in the Fred Astaire style uses a smart hat and a twirled cane.
explanation.definitionFit: A routine like 'Top Hat' is a dance, and such performances classically feature a dapper hat and a spinning cane.

clue.text: Like footballer Harry, tackling Chelsea's forward sideways

Harry Kane is England's football captain
the opening letter of the club name

explanation.surface: A striker challenging a Chelsea forward from the side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forward' looks like a player position; it is the first letter of the club.
explanation.definitionFit: Looking askance is looking sideways, often with suspicion.

clue.text: Footing cost up front (poor, taking on overdraft), touring Hawaii

indicators.note: up front points to the opening letter of the preceding word

touring means travelling around, so the preceding letters go around the next item

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
HI is the US postal abbreviation for Hawaii
ropy means of poor quality
OD is the banking abbreviation for overdrawn or overdraft

explanation.surface: Bills charged up front to a broke tourist travelling in Hawaii.
explanation.walkthrough: Ropy is British slang for shoddy or poor, and OD the bank-statement abbreviation for overdrawn. 'Footing' is playful: treatment of feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Chiropody is the medical care of feet, so a jokey 'footing' (attending to the foot) stands for it.

clue.text: Withdrawn, relieved, when son heads south

explanation.definitionFit: Atrial relates to an atrium of the heart, so it is cardiac in a partial sense, playfully 'somewhat hearty'.

clue.text: Support Bob in the Winter Olympics

taken as written
